messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Military Topics: Talks about military, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ahmed, a 64-year-old Middle Eastern man and former politician, has lived with the haunting memories of his time as a relief worker in a war zone for years. His experiences have profoundly impacted his daily life, leading him to seek psychological help after decades of coping through avoidance and distraction. The traumatic event that still haunts Ahmed occurred during a particularly volatile period when he was working in a war-torn city. One day, while distributing supplies, he witnessed a bombing that left the streets smoldering with the acrid smell of burnt rubber and metal. The explosion killed several civilians right before his eyes, including a young child who had been reaching out for help just moments earlier. The silence following the blast was deafening—a silence that felt even more terrifying than the cacophony of chaos. Since then, Ahmed has developed specific triggers that remind him of this horrific event. Interacting with strangers often brings back the sense of dread and vulnerability he felt in the war zone. He avoids talking to new people as much as possible, which has affected his ability to engage with constituents and colleagues in his political work. When military topics come up in conversation, Ahmed finds himself feeling overwhelmed and anxious, struggling to maintain composure. The olfactory cue—the smell of burnt materials—has been particularly difficult for him. Whenever he catches a whiff of something burning, it instantly transports him back to the scene of the bombing. This has led him to avoid areas with smoke or fire, even when there is no immediate danger. To cope with these intense feelings and memories, Ahmed employs several maladaptive strategies. He tries hard to control his emotions, often suppressing any signs of distress, which can lead to internal turmoil he struggles to express. When the memories start to overwhelm him, he distracts himself by throwing himself into work or other tasks. This overworking has taken a toll on both his health and personal relationships. Ahmed's belief that unusual silence indicates impending danger is deeply ingrained. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of threat and repeatedly checks that doors and windows are locked. These behaviors have become habitual, causing him to miss out on social interactions and relaxation time with friends who no longer understand why he seems so anxious all the time. The memories themselves remain fragmented and terrifying. When he tries to recall the event, pieces of it come back in disconnected flashes—images of the explosion, the smell of burning debris, the sound of shattering glass—all of which bring back the same overwhelming terror he felt at the time. This makes everyday life feel like a series of small triggers waiting to set off intense emotional responses. Over time, these coping mechanisms have led to significant consequences. His work as a politician has suffered due to his avoidance behaviors and overworking habits. Colleagues have noticed that he is more distant and less engaged in discussions, which has affected the collaborative nature of political work. Personal relationships are strained as well; friends find it hard to understand why Ahmed avoids social gatherings or conversations that might touch on military topics. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was a recent incident where the smell of burnt food in his home triggered a full-blown panic attack, leaving him unable to function for several hours. He realized he could no longer continue living this way, constantly on edge and unable to engage fully with life. Ahmed is most afraid that these memories will never truly leave him alone, haunting him forever. Yet, he also hopes that through therapy, he can find a way to manage his reactions and regain some semblance of normalcy in his daily life. He wants to be able to interact with people without fear, work effectively as a politician again, and enjoy the moments without being consumed by the past.
